  - Defense, Space & Security: $26,300 million (per the FY2022 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations)

Note: This report strictly contains factual data as requested. Further analysis or interpretation is not included.

flagged_claims.claim_text: Commercial Airplanes: $39,000 million (per the FY2020 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations)
flagged_claims.reason: This figure is implausibly high for Boeing's Commercial Airplanes segment in FY2020. This period was severely impacted by the 737 MAX grounding and the global COVID-19 pandemic, which drastically reduced air travel and new aircraft orders/deliveries. Revenue for this segment was known to be significantly lower in 2020 than in pre-pandemic years or even 2022. The reported figure suggests a boom, which is contrary to well-known historical events.

flagged_claims.claim_text: Commercial Airplanes: $12,426 million (per the FY2021 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations)
flagged_claims.reason: This figure seems implausibly low for FY2021, especially when compared to the reported FY2022 figure of $27,100 million. While 2021 was still challenging, a drop to this level from the (incorrectly reported) $39,000 million in 2020, followed by more than doubling to 2022, suggests an erratic and unlikely trend for a segment of this size. It also appears too low given the actual recovery trajectory for Boeing's commercial division.

flagged_claims.claim_text: Defense, Space & Security: $22,100 million (per the FY2021 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations)
flagged_claims.reason: This figure appears inconsistent with the reported revenues for the same segment in FY2020 ($26,400 million) and FY2022 ($26,300 million). Defense revenues are generally more stable than commercial, and a significant dip in 2021 followed by a recovery to nearly the 2020 level in 2022 without a clear external driver seems unusual.

flagged_claims.claim_text: Global Services: $19,162 million (per the FY22 10-K, Consolidated Statements of Operations)
flagged_claims.reason: This figure seems implausibly high for FY2020, especially when compared to the reported FY2021 ($18,525 million) and FY2022 ($16,300 million) figures, which show a declining trend. While Global Services can be more resilient, a peak in 2020 followed by a decline doesn't align with the general impact of COVID-19 on air travel and related services, which would likely have seen a dip or slower growth in 2020.
